title: Evaluating Generate–Validate–Repair Pipelines for Intent‑to‑Configuration NetOps Tasks: A Preregistered Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study comparing a baseline single‑shot LLM configuration generator against a guarded generate→validate→repair pipeline (with a canary stage) on a 1000‑task synthetic NetOps stress corpus (2000 paired episodes). The declared model was gpt‑5‑mini (provider: openai_responses) and validation used a deterministic digital‑twin validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Under preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics exactly one sampled initial generation per task was deterministically reused by both arms; downstream deterministic validation and the permitted single repair call (guarded arm only) were the only mechanisms for paired outcome differences. Observed outcomes: baseline safe‑deploy = 995/1000 = 0.995; guarded safe‑deploy = 1000/1000 = 1.000; paired difference = 0.005 (n11=995, n10=5, n01=0, n00=0). The preregistered primary inferential test (exact two‑sided McNemar) yields p = 0.0625 (not < 0.05). The preregistered secondary descriptive summary (paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI, 10,000 resamples, seed 1729) is [0.001, 0.01]. Only five validator‑triggered repairs occurred and total model calls used = 1005 (shared_initial = 1000; repair = 5). We report the exact McNemar result as the preregistered confirmatory outcome, present the bootstrap CI as a secondary descriptive summary, explicitly label a one‑sided McNemar (p = 0.03125) as exploratory/post‑hoc, and interpret the small absolute guarded benefit in light of sparse discordant counts, high baseline validity, validator scope, and the shared_initial_candidate design.

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→configuration translation for network operations promises reduced manual effort but raises safety risks: multi‑step sequencing errors, transient invariant violations, and protected‑field interference can convert plausible command sequences into harmful actions. Prior surveys and controlled studies document LLM hallucination, prompt sensitivity, and structured‑output failures that affect code and configuration generation, motivating architectures that pair generative models with deterministic validators and bounded repair procedures [1],[2].

This paper reports a preregistered, artifact‑grounded paired experiment that isolates purely downstream validator/repair effects under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Our precise research question is: when baseline and guarded conditions begin from the exact same sampled initial candidate (shared_initial_candidate semantics), to what degree can a downstream deterministic validator plus a single allowed repair call (guarded pipeline with a canary stage) improve paired safe‑deploy outcomes compared with reusing the same initial candidate unmodified (baseline)? The design intentionally isolates downstream interventions (validation and at‑most‑one repair) so that any paired difference is attributable to those downstream mechanisms rather than to first‑pass generation differences such as prompt engineering, constrained decoding, or sampling variance.

Contributions. (1) A preregistered paired experiment (Npairs = 1000) with deterministic task selection from a challenging synthetic workflow stress corpus and archived validator traces. (2) Full execution accounting and explicit recording of model configuration (declared model = gpt‑5‑mini; recorded temperature = null/unset — null/unset is not evidence of deterministic hosted‑model sampling and does not imply temperature = 0). (3) Transparent confirmation that the preregistered primary test (exact two‑sided McNemar) did not reach two‑sided α = 0.05 (p = 0.0625), accompanied by preregistered secondary descriptive summaries (paired bootstrap CI = [0.001, 0.01], bootstrap_seed = 1729) and explicit labelling of any one‑sided tests as exploratory because they were not prespecified in the frozen preregistration.
sections.related_work:
Empirical and survey literature documents frequent hallucinations, prompt sensitivity, and errors that degrade correctness for code and configuration tasks, motivating verifier‑augmented architectures [1],[2]. Constrained decoding and schema‑aware planning reduce syntactic and executable errors in structured domains, though many demonstrations originate outside NetOps and therefore depend on validator/tool fidelity when adapted to network workflows [3]. Recent NetOps and agentic‑AI system papers emphasize verifier‑assisted repair, guarded architectures, and governance/proof‑carrying proposals to mitigate automation risks; these works present prototypes and argue that operational reliability depends on validator coverage and externally enforced protocols rather than on any single model alone [4],[5],[6].

Our study complements this literature by preregistering a paired comparison whose estimand isolates the incremental effect of deterministic downstream validation and a single limited repair call when the initial candidate is held constant across conditions. This avoids conflating downstream interventions with first‑pass prompt/decoding differences and clarifies the contribution and limits of validation+repair layers under tightly controlled conditions.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and frozen design. The study preregistration (study id cand‑003‑stud‑001) was finalized and frozen prior to any hosted‑model invocation and the preregistration is recorded in the archived execution manifest. Key preregistered elements: confirmatory paired binary design; task_count = 1000 deterministic tasks drawn from a synthetic challenging corpus; generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate (exactly one sampled initial generation per pair deterministically reused by both conditions); initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1; maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1; primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; primary test = exact two‑sided McNemar. Secondary preregistered summaries: paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729) and sensitivity analyses treating failed calls as unsafe.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics and interpretive consequences. Under generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate both baseline and guarded episodes begin from the same sampled initial candidate; the guarded pipeline may reject the candidate via deterministic validation and may invoke at most one permitted repair call. Under this design, paired outcome differences can only arise from deterministic validator decisions and permitted repair(s). The design therefore does not measure effects that would arise from independent first‑pass generations, alternative prompts, or constrained decoding arms that were not executed.

Model/runtime configuration and temperature caveat. The declared provider/model is gpt‑5‑mini (provider: openai_responses). The recorded model configuration shows temperature = null/unset; null/unset is not evidence of deterministic hosted‑model sampling and does not imply temperature = 0. The orchestration/adapter family was hosted_netops_gvr_v1 and validation used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator version 5.0). The validator enforces workflow policies, required command presence and order, protected‑field noninterference, and returns a deterministic binary safe‑deploy verdict per task manifest.

Task corpus, selection rule, and validator semantics. Tasks were selected deterministically using the preregistered ordinal rule producing exactly 1000 unique tasks. Each task manifest contains initial_state, expected_final_state, required_sequence, allowed_touched_fields, and difficulty labels. The deterministic_netops_validator_v5 compares parsed candidate command sequences against manifest constraints in a deterministic digital‑twin emulator and emits structured validator traces; scoring used a rule that produces a binary validity outcome required for the paired analysis.

Execution accounting, retries, and missingness. The preregistration limited retries (maximum_attempts_per_call = 1) and prespecified missingness treatments. Execution completed without failed episodes. The preregistered 'complete_pair_primary' missingness treatment was applied; sensitivity analyses treating failures as unsafe were preregistered but not required because failed episodes = 0.

Statistical analysis plan and prespecification fidelity. The preregistered confirmatory procedure is the exact two‑sided McNemar test on the 2×2 contingency table of paired outcomes. The paired bootstrap percentile interval (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) was preregistered as a descriptive secondary summary. The preregistration did not prespecify a one‑sided McNemar; any one‑sided McNemar reported below is explicitly labeled exploratory/post‑hoc and does not affect the preregistered confirmatory inference. Multiplicity adjustments for secondary hypotheses were prespecified for any additional hypothesis claims; we make no additional confirmatory claims here.
sections.results:
Execution and accounting. Planned episodes = 2000; completed = 2000; complete_pairs = 1000; failed episodes = 0. Provider call audit recorded a total of 1005 hosted model call events: 1000 shared initial generations and 5 repair invocations. All deterministic consistency checks passed and no cross‑condition cache reuse was observed.

Primary paired outcomes and preregistered inferential test. The observed 2×2 paired contingency table is: n11 = 995 (both succeeded), n10 = 5 (guarded succeeded, baseline failed), n01 = 0 (baseline succeeded, guarded failed), n00 = 0 (both failed). Observed success rates: baseline = 995/1000 = 0.995; guarded = 1000/1000 = 1.000; observed paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.005. The preregistered primary confirmatory test (exact two‑sided McNemar) returns p = 0.0625; this does not meet the preregistered two‑sided α = 0.05 threshold, so the preregistered H1 is not supported.

Preregistered secondary descriptive summaries and sensitivity. The preregistered paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) yields [0.001, 0.01]. The bootstrap interval excludes zero because bootstrap resampling with extremely sparse discordant counts can produce nonzero percentile bounds; the bootstrap summary was preregistered as descriptive only and is sensitive to small n10/n01 counts. An exploratory one‑sided McNemar (guarded > baseline), which was not prespecified, yields p = 0.03125 and is reported as post‑hoc/exploratory only.

Repair mechanics and representative diagnostics. Only five validator‑triggered repairs occurred. Representative validator traces show initial candidates rejected for required_sequence violations or protected‑interface touches, a single permitted repair call invoked, and a repaired candidate accepted after revalidation. Total model calls used = 1005 (shared_initial = 1000; repair = 5).

Contamination, exclusions, and missingness. Contamination checks and exclusion rules found no prompt‑leakage flags and no deterministic emulator errors. No post‑hoc exclusions were applied. All seeds and task_index selection rules were fixed pre‑execution per the preregistration.

Additional diagnostic interpretation. The small number of discordant pairs explains the discrete McNemar p‑value boundary behavior (exact McNemar with n10=5, n01=0 yields p = 0.0625 two‑sided), demonstrating limited sensitivity when baseline validity is near unity.
sections.discussion:
Confirmatory vs descriptive outcomes and preregistration fidelity. The preregistered primary inference is the exact two‑sided McNemar (p = 0.0625), so H1 is not supported at two‑sided α = 0.05. The paired bootstrap CI ([0.001, 0.01]) is a preregistered descriptive summary and excludes zero due to bootstrap sensitivity with extremely sparse discordant pairs; this descriptive statistic does not overturn the preregistered confirmatory result. The one‑sided McNemar (p = 0.03125) is exploratory/post‑hoc and was not prespecified.

Power assumption mismatch and interpretive consequences. The preregistered power plan assumed baseline ≈ 0.60 and targeted an absolute increase of 0.15 to achieve >80% power at two‑sided α = 0.05. The observed baseline success rate (0.995) is far higher than that assumption; this mismatch substantially reduces the study's sensitivity to detect small absolute gains because near‑unity baseline rates produce very few discordant pairs. Thus the lack of two‑sided significance at α = 0.05 reflects limited statistical power in the observed regime rather than definitive evidence of no practical benefit in settings with higher baseline failure prevalence.

Mechanistic implications within shared_initial_candidate semantics. Under the shared_initial_candidate design, only downstream validation and permitted repairs can create paired differences. The five observed repairs demonstrate that a validator with suitable coverage can correct particular ordering/sequence violations. However, the low repair invocation count may reflect (a) few initial candidate violations in the synthetic corpus, (b) generator behavior for the chosen model+prompt producing valid candidates, or (c) validator coverage that does not capture other semantic error classes. Distinguishing these mechanisms requires follow‑ups that vary generator semantics, repair budget, and validator rule sets.

Threats to validity. Construct validity: the safe‑deploy binary depends on deterministic_netops_validator_v5 rule coverage; omitted policy checks would inflate measured success. Internal validity: shared_initial_candidate semantics isolate downstream effects but preclude measuring prompt/decoding interventions. External validity: the synthetic task corpus and single model (gpt‑5‑mini) limit generalization to heterogeneous production environments and other model families. Conclusion validity: extreme baseline success yields sparse discordant counts, reducing power for exact paired tests.

Operational implications and recommended follow‑ups. Artifact‑grounded evidence shows verifier‑guided repair can avert some unsafe outcomes in synthetic workflow settings, but measurable marginal gains depend on baseline failure prevalence, validator sensitivity/coverage, and permitted repair budget. Preregistered follow‑ups we recommend: (1) evaluate independent first‑pass generation arms to measure prompt/decoding intervention effects; (2) sweep repair budgets (0..k repairs) to quantify marginal returns per failure class; (3) expand validator rule suites and topology heterogeneity to probe external validity; and (4) include multiple model families to map model dependence. Each follow‑up should align power calculations to plausible baseline failure rates and specify confirmatory analyses a priori.
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired study with shared_initial_candidate semantics on a 1000‑task synthetic NetOps stress corpus, a guarded generate→validate→repair pipeline produced a small absolute paired improvement (0.005) relative to a baseline single‑shot generator; the preregistered exact two‑sided McNemar test did not reach α = 0.05 (p = 0.0625). Only five validator repairs were invoked and total model calls used = 1005. The primary inferential outcome is the preregistered exact McNemar result; a one‑sided McNemar (p = 0.03125) was computed post‑hoc and is explicitly labeled exploratory because it was not prespecified in the frozen preregistration. These artifact‑grounded results indicate that downstream verifier/repair safeguards can prevent some unsafe outcomes, but measurable marginal gains are constrained when baseline outputs are already highly valid and when the paired design isolates downstream effects. Full preregistration, execution manifests, raw responses, validator traces, and analysis artifacts are archived with the run to support reproducibility and to guide preregistered follow‑ups that broaden model diversity, validator coverage, and repair budgets.

This visualization supplements the preregistered exact McNemar confirmatory test and illustrates bootstrap sensitivity to sparse discordant counts.

Orchestration and validator: hosted_netops_gvr_v1 with deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as the validator/digital twin. Preregistration: study cand‑003‑stud‑001 (frozen prior to any model calls and recorded in the archived execution manifest). Immutable initial master prompt reference archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Human role and autonomy boundary: after the autonomy lock the research run executed the preregistered experiment, analysis, and manuscript drafting; no human manually edited the manuscript technical content after the autonomy lock.
limitations: Single‑model scope: only the declared model gpt‑5‑mini was evaluated; results do not generalize across model families or versions.

Synthetic corpus and deterministic validator: tasks come from a synthetic stress corpus and validation used a deterministic digital twin (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); external validity to heterogeneous vendor/legacy environments is limited.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired comparison isolates downstream validator/repair effects only; it does not measure differences that would arise from independent first‑pass generations or alternative prompting arms that were not executed (those arms were not part of the frozen preregistration).

Low baseline failure prevalence: baseline success = 99.5%; the preregistered power plan assumed baseline≈0.60 and a target effect of 0.15, so the observed baseline greatly reduces sensitivity to detect small absolute gains. This mismatch is reported explicitly and reduces the study's ability to detect very small practical effects using the preregistered confirmatory test.
Sparse repairs and interpretation limits: only five validator repairs were invoked, constraining inference about repair efficacy across failure modes.

Statistical nuance: the preregistered primary test is exact two‑sided McNemar (p = 0.0625). The paired bootstrap percentile CI [0.001, 0.01] is a preregistered descriptive summary but is sensitive to sparse discordant counts; a one‑sided McNemar (p = 0.03125) was computed post‑hoc and is explicitly labeled exploratory because it was not prespecified in the frozen preregistration.

Construct validity: the safe‑deploy binary depends on the emulator/validator's rule set; semantic and emergent multi‑device policy violations may be underrepresented in the validator's modeled constraints.
